query: For high-entropy-alloy coatings used in wear-resistant applications, what single intervention could improve wear resistance across operating temperatures? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its expected mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise identical unmodified coating, the temperature and sliding conditions under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment with a clear result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the power of atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) can improve the wear resistance of high-entropy-alloy coatings across operating temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy coatings on low carbon steel substrates
generation.intervention: Increasing the power of atmospheric plasma spraying (APS)
generation.conditions: Operating temperatures ranging from room temperature to high temperatures (up to 750 °C), under dry sliding wear conditions with varying normal loads and sliding speeds
generation.structural_mediator: Dense microstructure with reduced porosity and the formation of a lubricating layer consisting of multi-component metal oxides
generation.mechanism: The increased APS power enhances the melting rate and alloying process, reducing porosity and improving coating density, which in turn improves wear resistance by preventing severe adhesion wear and promoting the formation of a lubricating layer
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved wear resistance across operating temperatures, with a potential reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate
generation.baseline: Unmodified AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy coatings with lower APS power
generation.boundary: The improvement in wear resistance may be limited by the formation of complex phases or intermetallics at high temperatures, which can reduce ductility and lead to brittle behavior
generation.uncertainty: The exact relationship between APS power and wear resistance across different operating temperatures and conditions is not fully understood and requires further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Comparative study of wear resistance between high-entropy-alloy coatings fabricated with different APS power levels, under controlled operating temperatures and sliding conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the wear resistance of the coatings fabricated with higher APS power is not significantly improved compared to those fabricated with lower APS power, under the same operating conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified

Question: How does the power of atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) influence the microstructure, frictional wear resistance, and corrosion resistance of AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy coatings?. System: AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy coatings (HEACs) on low carbon steel (45#) substrates. Processing: Atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) using mechanically milled powders (15–50 μm) with four power levels (H1 < H2 < H3 < H4); H4 utilized the highest hydrogen-gas flow rate and power. Test conditions: Tribological tests: Si3N4 ball (5 mm), 5 N load, 1200 s sliding time; Corrosion tests: 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution, room temperature, 240 h immersion, potentiodynamic polarization, EIS (100 kHz–10 MHz). System: Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti-Ag (HEA-Ag) and Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti (HEC) coatings formed on carbon steel. Processing: Plasma spraying. Test conditions: Temperature range from 25 to 750 °C; ball-on-disk sliding; counterface not explicitly named in the specific Li et al. summary but implied standard tribological testing. Paper card. Question: How does grain size influence the tribological behavior, wear mechanisms, and wear resistance of CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloys under varying normal loads and sliding speeds?. System: CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy (HEA) with fine grain (FG, ~2.9 μm) and coarse grain (CG, ~63.4 μm) microstructures. Processing: Arc-melting of pure metals followed by drop-casting into a copper mold, forging at 1000 °C, cold rolling (80% reduction), and annealing at 800 °C for 30 min (FG) or 1000 °C for 60 min (CG). Test conditions: Reciprocating sliding friction against a 10 mm Si3N4 ball under dry conditions at room temperature; normal loads of 5 N and 30 N; sliding speeds of 1, 5, and 10 mm/s; sliding time of 1200 s.
